## New Cross-Domain Connection

- **[2026-11-05] Today's podcast pick, *The Doctor's Kitchen*, gives the recipe recommender the health-led chef it has never had. The host is a GP who cooks, and the episode the pick suggests starting with is Tommy Wood, the author of Health's main dementia source.** [[podcasts/suggestions]] (week of 2026-11-05) recommends Dr Rupy Aujla's show. Its suggested first episode is Wood's "7 habits a neuroscientist swears by" (Mar 2026). Wood also wrote the Ferriss guest post behind [[health/source-wood-brain-sharp-2026]], but the pick never says so and frames the show as a follow-on to the Candow creatine episode instead. The Cooking side is the gap: the recipe recommender says it is "inspired by Fred's chef profiles", and [[cooking/chefs]] lists only four, Quinn, Slater, Bourdain and Chang. None of them cooks to a health target, which fits the 10-09 idea's finding that only two of the first 42 suggestions were oily-fish mains. Aujla publishes recipes built around exactly this kind of target (his Doctor's Kitchen cookbooks; general knowledge, not from a wiki source). **Why it matters:** a fifth chef page for Aujla in [[cooking/chefs]] is the smallest change that would steer the Friday batch toward Health without rewriting the recommender prompt or waiting for [[health/my-protocol]]'s Diet section to be filled in. Listening to the Wood episode first would also show whether his advice has changed since the April source page, which is still the wiki's only dementia-diet reference.

## New Cross-Domain Connection

- **[2026-11-04] Two pages filed on 11-03 show that "AI is raising productivity" and "AI vendors' economics are getting worse" can both be true at once. The gains are going to the companies that use AI and cut staff, not to the model vendors. Fred's AI checks don't yet ask which side of that split a company is on.** [[ai-tech/source-bloomberg-ai-productivity-bet-2026-05-11]] reports US labour productivity averaging over 2% a year for 2020-26, so Robert Gordon concedes his bet against Brynjolfsson. It also says the gains show up as Meta, Microsoft and Amazon cutting jobs to fund capex, with 95% of firms seeing no measurable AI ROI (MIT NANDA). [[finance/investor-letters/source-burry-anthropic-s1-2026-10-27]] shows the supplier side moving the other way over the same months: Anthropic's revenue per compute dollar fell from $2.08 to $1.70, sequential growth dropped from 144% to ~45%, and Microsoft (one of the companies cutting jobs) reportedly cut planned Claude spend by over a third. In other words, the buyer keeps the productivity gain as margin and bargains down the vendor. The "Burry Signal" table in [[finance/trading-portfolio]] tests for bubble exposure, and the 09-29 connection added a disruption test. Neither asks who keeps the gain. Under that test the three puts (ORCL, NBIS, PLTR: compute and AI-software suppliers) sit on the losing side, and so does any holding that charges by seat or hour (ACN, ADBE). Labour-heavy users with pricing power, like UPS in the paper book (revenue per piece +6.1% on volume −3%), sit on the winning side. **Dated check:** Burry says Anthropic's S-1 amendment with Q3 and October run-rate figures comes before the roadshow. When it is filed, record three numbers: revenue per compute dollar (still ≤1.70?), monthly growth against his 4.3% break-even rate, and any cut to hyperscaler commitments. These three are the first hard test of the supplier-side thesis behind all three puts. Use them in the hold/close rule the 11-03 ORCL idea asks for. Do not use "ITM" alone. (Note: Claude, which maintains this wiki, is made by Anthropic; this entry restates Burry's and Bloomberg's figures without judging them.)
